hints: Focus on what type of oxide gives an acidic solution with water, this immediately points you toward non-metal oxides rather than metals like aluminium.
Think about how many water molecules each common Period 3 oxide needs, most need only one water per oxide molecule to make its acid.
Recall the large phosphorus(V) oxide molecule with four P atoms, and check how many waters it needs to make four molecules of phosphoric acid.
walkthrough:
**Use the acidic product clue**

Great start, an oxide that reacts with water to make an acid must be an acidic, non-metal oxide.

That rules out basic or insoluble amphoteric oxides straight away.

**Write the normal 1 to 1 reactions**

Most familiar non-metal oxides need just one water.

For example:
$$\text{SO}_{3} + \text{H}_{2}\text{O} \rightarrow \text{H}_{2}\text{SO}_{4}$$
$$\text{CO}_{2} + \text{H}_{2}\text{O} \rightarrow \text{H}_{2}\text{CO}_{3}$$

So a 1 to 6 ratio is very unusual and special.

**Spot the phosphorus(V) oxide reaction**

Phosphorus(V) oxide exists as the big molecule $\text{P}_{4}\text{O}_{10}$. It is powerfully acidic and hydrolysed by water:
$$\text{P}_{4}\text{O}_{10} + 6\text{H}_{2}\text{O} \rightarrow 4\text{H}_{3}\text{PO}_{4}$$

One molecule needs exactly six molecules of water to make four molecules of phosphoric acid, $\text{H}_{3}\text{PO}_{4}$, which is acidic. This matches perfectly, so Z is phosphorus.

options.A: Aluminium oxide, $\text{Al}_{2}\text{O}_{3}$, is amphoteric and essentially insoluble. It does not react with water to form an acid, so it cannot give a 1 to 6 reaction.
options.B: Phosphorus(V) oxide, $\text{P}_{4}\text{O}_{10}$, reacts as $\text{P}_{4}\text{O}_{10} + 6\text{H}_{2}\text{O} \rightarrow 4\text{H}_{3}\text{PO}_{4}$. One oxide molecule uses six waters to form acidic phosphoric acid, exactly as described.
options.C: Silicon dioxide, $\text{SiO}_{2}$, is acidic but it is a giant covalent solid that does not react with water under normal conditions. It does not form silicic acid this way.
options.D: Sulfur oxides give acids but in a 1 to 1 ratio, for example $\text{SO}_{3} + \text{H}_{2}\text{O} \rightarrow \text{H}_{2}\text{SO}_{4}$. Students who remember sulfur makes strong acids may pick this, but the 6 waters do not fit.
